name: Neptune's Fountain
label: Neptune's Fountain
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/240120228: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fontanna Neptuna' (9 m across).
notes: Bronze 17th-century fountain at the heart of the Long Market.

text.description: Neptune's Fountain stands on the Długi Targ (Long Market), right in front of the entrance to the Artus Court, and is one of the best-known landmarks of Gdańsk. The bronze sea god with his trident stands on a stem of black tuff, surrounded by a decorative fence. It photographs well because the figure is a clear, dark shape against the pale, tall town-house fronts of the Long Market, and the fence and basin give you something to build a foreground around. The figure was designed by Abraham van den Blocke and made by Peter Husen, then cast in bronze in 1615. It weighs 650 kilograms. The fountain was not opened until 9 October 1633, after delays that included a war and the designer's death. In 1634 it was given a fence with gilded Polish Eagles. The Rococo details date from rebuilding work between 1757 and 1761. It was damaged in the Second World War, restored after it, and fully renovated again in 2011-2012. For your own photos, stay back a little and let the buildings frame the statue instead of cropping tightly. Pick a moment when few people are passing in front of it, or include a few on purpose to show the scale of the square.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Gdańsk, on the Długi Targ (Long Market), directly in front of the Artus Court.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Long Market area in the centre of Gdańsk, or come by taxi or hired scooter. From there the fountain is directly to the south. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the fountain with the buildings around it. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of Neptune and his trident, since you are standing about 79 m away.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there the fountain sits in the middle of the Long Market, with the surrounding buildings behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the statue on one of the vertical lines, with the building fronts filling the background. Try one wide shot with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene, then zoom in for a detail shot of the figure. Keep the camera level so the tall buildings do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bronze figure to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the statue does not turn into a silhouette. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a dramatic, close-up view, as it will push the fountain far into the distance from this spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people in the square. In the evening, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or post if the buildings are lit.

text.access_note: The fountain stands in the open on the Long Market; if you also want to go inside the Artus Court, check the official site before you go.

name: St. Mary's Church
label: St. Mary's Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'ulica Mariacka' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of ulica Mariacka nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/46426385: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St Mary’s Church' (129 m across).
notes: One of the largest brick churches in the world.

text.description: St. Mary's Church is the huge brick church that dominates central Gdańsk. It was completed in 1502 in the Brick Gothic style and is counted among the largest brick churches in the world. Locals call it the Crown of Gdańsk. The building is about 105 metres long, so from close by it is too big to fit in one frame. That is why the street approach works so well. The best classic view is along ulica Mariacka, a cobbled street that runs from the church down towards the Motława river. Looking along it towards the church, the dark brick walls close off the end of the street, with house fronts and porches on either side acting as a natural frame. The church has a long history. Building began on the present church in 1379, and the Baroque Royal Chapel next to it was finished in 1681. For a phone photo, keep the church in the middle of the frame and let the street lead the eye towards it. Hold the phone level, because tilting it upwards makes the tower lean. Wait a moment for people to pass, or include a few of them to show the scale of the street. The tower viewing terrace is a separate, ticketed experience and not part of this ground-level view, so check the official site before you go if you want to go up.
text.geographic_location: In central Gdańsk, at the head of ulica Mariacka, which runs down towards the Motława river.
text.directions_text: There are no tram or railway stops listed for this spot, so head for central Gdańsk and make your way on foot to ulica Mariacka. It is about 54 metres east of the church, so the church is to the west of you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the street and the church together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the house fronts and the tower. Use 2x or more if your phone has a telephoto lens, for a tighter shot of the church closing off the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on ulica Mariacka (looking back up the street from the Motława end, toward the church). The brick church closes the end of the cobbled street, framed by the historic house fronts and porches on either side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the street in the centre, so the church sits at the vanishing point and the house fronts balance left and right. Keep the phone upright and level so the verticals stay straight. For a different angle, try ulica Piwna, where narrow facades lead the eye towards the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the brick keeps its colour. If people are walking through, a Live Photo lets you pick the frame with the fewest passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning is usually calmer on the street. In the afternoon the church may be backlit, so check the screen and adjust the exposure.

text.access_note: The street is an open public space, but the church is a place of worship and the tower terrace is a separate visit, so check the official site before you go for visiting rules.

name: Museum of the Second World War
label: WWII Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plac Władysława Bartoszewskiego' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plac Władysława Bartoszewskiego' (way/460826216): middle (221 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6808053: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museum of the Second World War' (178 m across).
notes: Striking tilted modern building with a large underground exhibition.

text.description:
The Museum of the Second World War is one of the most striking modern buildings in Gdańsk, and it is easy to photograph from the square in front of it. The best-known feature is the 40-metre leaning tower with a glass façade. It is the red-tiled tilted tower you see rising above the entrance, and the rubble-filled wall below it makes a strong foreground. Together they give you a ready-made picture: a rough, dark base, a bright tilted tower and a wide open plaza in front.

The museum was set up in 2008 and its exhibits opened to the public in 2017. The building was designed by the Gdynia-based Kwadrat studio, covers roughly 23,000 square metres and is made up of three main spheres. Its seat faces the Motława River on Wałowa Street, close to the Radunia Canal and the historic Polish Post Office Building. A statue of Witold Pilecki was added in front of the museum in 2019, which gives you a human-scale detail if you want one.

Step back or use the ultra-wide lens to fit the tower in, and keep your phone level so the tower's lean looks deliberate and not like a tilted horizon. If the entrance is busy, a second option is Ołowianka, across the Motława canal. From there the angular tower appears as a distant shape, away from the crowds.
text.geographic_location: In central Gdańsk on Wałowa Street, facing the Motława River. It stands close to the Radunia Canal and the historic Polish Post Office Building.
text.directions_text: There are no tram or railway stops right at this spot, so head for Plac Władysława Bartoszewskiego on Wałowa Street, near the Radunia Canal and the historic Polish Post Office Building. Follow the compass direction on the map for the last few steps. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the tower, the rubble wall and the plaza together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier shot of the tower above the entrance. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the texture of the rubble and steel-mesh wall or for the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plac Władysława Bartoszewskiego (in front of the main entrance, facing the building). The red-tiled, tilted tower of the museum rising above the rubble-filled entrance wall, with the plaza in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the wall with the vertical lines, so that only the tower itself appears to lean. Keep some plaza in the bottom of the frame to give a sense of scale. For a calmer, more distant view of the tower, try Ołowianka across the Motława canal as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the red tiles stay rich. Do not rely on portrait mode for the building. It works better for a person standing in front of the wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light in the early morning or late afternoon usually flatters the red tiles and the rough wall. Going early also tends to mean fewer people in front of the entrance.

text.access_note: The square in front of the museum is an open public space.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft early-morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the red tiles and the rubble wall.
The area in front of the entrance tends to be quieter early in the day.
Tilting the phone or standing too close can make the tower's lean look accidental; gridlines help keep verticals straight.
The entrance square is open to the public without a ticket.

name: European Solidarity Centre
label: Solidarity Centre
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/179780270: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Solidarity Museum (European Solidarity Centre)' (158 m across).
notes: Rusty-steel museum building by the shipyard gate with a rooftop viewing terrace.

text.description: The European Solidarity Centre is a museum and library in Gdańsk about the history of Solidarity, the Polish trade union and civil resistance movement, and other opposition movements in Communist Eastern Europe. It opened on 31 August 2014, the anniversary of the 1980 Gdańsk Agreement. The building was designed by FORT Architects, who won an international competition in 2007. Its walls are meant to recall the hulls of ships built at the Gdańsk Shipyard, and that is what makes it work for a phone photo: the big, plain, sloping surfaces give you strong shapes and clean lines, and a few people walking past show how large it is. The outline of the building is about 158 m across, so you will not fit all of it in at the default lens (1x) from close up. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole front, and the default lens (1x) for a calmer view of one section. Switch on the gridlines to keep the long edges straight, and move a step or two sideways until the walls do not lean. The 2x telephoto, if your phone has it, suits details such as the join between two wall sections or a single window. The centre holds around 2,000 exhibits and about 100,000 books and documents, so it is also somewhere to spend time once you have your pictures. Check the official site before you go, in case access to parts of the building or the grounds is limited.
text.geographic_location: In Gdańsk, Poland. Its walls evoke the hulls of ships built at the Gdańsk Shipyard.
text.directions_text: No tram stop or station is listed for this spot, so use the map to find the building, for example by taxi, and ask for the Europejskie Centrum Solidarności. Once you arrive, look at the map and walk to the phone icon on the map, which is at the middle of the building's outline. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full width of the building, then use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), save it for details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up one long edge of the wall with a horizontal line. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. Include a person or two for scale. For a variation, stand low and shoot along the wall so the lines lead away from you.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wall to focus, then slide the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its detail instead of turning into a silhouette.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to large walls than midday sun. On a cloudy day the surfaces photograph evenly.

text.access_note: The surroundings can be photographed from outside, but the museum and library are an official visitor site, so check the official site before you go.

name: Long Market (Długi Targ)
label: Long Market
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-16: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: The main square of the Royal Way, lined with colourful merchant houses.

text.description: Long Market (Długi Targ) is the broad, street-like square at the heart of Gdańsk's old centre. It runs from the end of Ulica Długa (the Long Lane) to the Green Gate, and it forms part of the Royal Route. It photographs well because it is one long, open space with tall, narrow town houses on both sides, so the eye is led straight along it. The market dates to about the 13th century, when it began as a merchant road. The Latin name Longa Platea first appears in 1331. For centuries Polish monarchs entered the city this way on ceremonial visits, and the wealthiest citizens lived along it, which helps explain the grand frontages. Use that for a wider, scene-setting shot and let the telephoto bring the square closer. If you want details such as doorways, carved facades and street life, walk to the square itself and shoot from there. Keep your phone upright for the tall facades and turn it sideways for the long view along the street. Check that the gridlines are on so the rooflines stay level.
text.geographic_location: Long Market sits in the centre of Gdańsk, at the end of Ulica Długa, next to the Green Gate.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so make your way on foot to the Green Gate end of Ulica Długa. The phone icon on the map is about 100 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to see how the view looks, then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the distant square closer. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only once you are in the square itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 100 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the gridlines to keep the rooflines straight and place the length of the square along one of the lower lines. Include some foreground for depth, and keep the tall house fronts at the edges of the frame. In the square itself, the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens helps you fit the full height of the facades in.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the buildings to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky and pale walls do not wash out. Hold the phone with both hands when you use the telephoto, as zoomed shots show shake more.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is likely to suit the view from here, when the sun is behind you and falls on the house fronts. Early in the day the square is also usually less crowded.

text.access_note: The Long Market is a public square, but check the official site before you go if you plan to visit any museum or building around it.

name: Artus Court
label: Artus Court
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Długi Targ' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Długi Targ' (relation/5537950): middle (225 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/60064071: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Artus Court' (39 m across).
notes: Gothic merchants' hall with a grand interior and a huge tiled stove.

text.description: Artus Court is the grand merchants' meeting house on Długi Targ (the Long Market), in the middle of Gdańsk's historic centre. It was once the place where wealthy traders and visiting foreigners gathered in the evenings, and today it is a branch of the Gdańsk History Museum. It photographs well because the tall, richly decorated front rises straight out of the pedestrian square, and Neptune's Fountain stands just in front of it, which gives you a natural foreground. The façade was rebuilt in 1617 by Abraham van den Blocke in the style of Dutch Mannerism. It carries statues of antique heroes, allegories of strength and justice, and a figure of Fortuna on the gable. Inside is a Gothic hall with an 11-metre tiled stove made in the 1540s. The building was badly damaged in 1945 and rebuilt after the war. For the classic view, stand on the square with the fountain in front of you and the façade rising behind it. Then step closer and use zoom to pick out the statues and portal medallions. The square is busy in peak season, so a patient pause between groups helps. If you plan to go inside, check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Artus Court stands at Długi Targ 44, in the centre of Gdańsk, on the Long Market. Neptune's Fountain is on the same square, directly in front of it.
text.directions_text: Start from the historic centre of Gdańsk and walk to the Long Market (Długi Targ). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the classic view of fountain and façade together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the square is crowded and you cannot step back. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the statues and gable details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Długi Targ (in front of the court, with Neptune's Fountain in the foreground). The classic postcard view: Neptune's Fountain in the foreground with the ornate Artus Court facade rising across the Long Market. Face north-west so Neptune's Fountain sits in the foreground and the ornate Artus Court façade rises across the Long Market behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the fountain on the lower third, with the façade filling the upper part. Keep your phone level so the building's vertical lines stay straight. Then zoom in for a second shot of the statues and the portal. This is the only viewpoint we recommend for the exterior.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the carved detail stays clear. In the evening, try night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a solid surface.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or evening, for golden-hour light and the lit-up façade.

text.access_note: The square outside is open public space, but the interior is a museum, so check the official site before you go.

name: Mariacka Street
label: Mariacka Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Brama Mariacka' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Brama Mariacka' (way/96723943): middle (30 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM W484239679 (Mariacka): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Cobbled lane with terraces, gargoyles and amber shops.

text.description: Mariacka Street is a narrow cobbled lane in Gdansk, lined with tall, dark townhouses with gabled fronts and gargoyle terraces. At the far end stands St Mary's Basilica. It photographs well because the street is a natural tunnel: the buildings on both sides lead the eye straight to the church. The best-known view is from the gate at the waterfront end, Brama Mariacka. Its arch acts as a frame around the street, the houses and the basilica behind them. This gives a tidier picture than shooting from the middle of the street. The street is pedestrian and open, so these views are free. Crowds build up through the day, so early morning is the usual advice if you want the cobbles empty. For a different view, walk to the Motława waterfront and look back at the gate and the row of old townhouses beside it. Blue hour or early morning gives a reflection in the water. Many shops along the street don't allow photos inside, so keep your pictures to the street itself. Take one frame from inside the gate looking up the street, then walk up toward the basilica and turn round for the reverse view, with the gabled houses converging toward the gate.
text.geographic_location: Mariacka Street runs between the Motława waterfront and St Mary's Basilica in Gdansk. The gate at the waterfront end is the usual starting point.
text.directions_text: No tram or rail stop is listed for this spot, so use a taxi or walk to the Motława waterfront beside Brama Mariacka. From there the street runs west toward St Mary's Basilica, about 2 minutes on foot to the middle of the street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from inside the gate so the arch frames the street. If you can't fit the whole arch in, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) and keep the phone level. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for pulling the basilica closer to the houses.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Brama Mariacka (Stand inside the gate and face up the street toward the basilica). The cobbled street framed by the gate's arch, with the dark townhouse facades on both sides and St. Mary's Basilica at the far end.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and centre the street between the two rows of houses, keeping the phone straight so the walls don't lean. Let the arch make a border around the picture. For another view, shoot the gate and the townhouses reflected in the Motława from the waterfront, or look back down the street from near the basilica.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the street or the church to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky at the end of the street doesn't wash out. In the shade of the gate, Night mode may switch on by itself, so hold still for the full exposure. Live Photos can catch passers-by, but a still frame is better for an empty street.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the street is quiet and empty. Blue hour or early morning also suits the reflection view from the waterfront.

text.access_note: Mariacka Street is a pedestrian public street and the views are free, but many shops don't allow photos inside.

name: Gdańsk Crane
label: Gdańsk Crane
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/96702317: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Brama Żuraw' (35 m across).
notes: Medieval wooden port crane, symbol of the city.

text.description: The Gdańsk Crane (Żuraw) is a 15th-century port crane on the Motława river, in the middle of the old city. Two tall, thick brick towers stand either side of a big wooden crane frame that reaches out over the water. It was finished by 1444 and was the largest port crane in medieval Europe. Today it is about 30 metres high, roughly 2 metres taller than the original. It photographs well because the dark brick and timber stand out against the water, and the shape is easy to recognise even in a small frame. The crane was badly damaged in 1945 and rebuilt between 1956 and 1959. After a long renovation it reopened on 30 April 2024. It now houses a branch of the National Maritime Museum. Start with a wide, straight-on view along the waterfront. Then move in for a second shot of the timber crane frame and the brick arch below it. Keep your phone upright to catch the full height of the towers. If any water is visible in front of the crane, include it in the frame. Moored boats or people strolling along the quay add scale.
text.geographic_location: In central Gdańsk, on the bank of the Motława river, at the point where Szeroka Street meets the water. It is one of the old city's waterside gates.
text.directions_text: Head for the Motława waterfront in central Gdańsk, close to the end of Szeroka Street; by taxi or hired scooter is easiest. From there the crane is 77 m to the north, about 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 60 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole crane with some river around it. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you have to stand close, and keep the towers straight. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the timber frame and brickwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 60 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the two brick towers up with the vertical lines. Keep the crane slightly off-centre and include any water visible in front of the crane. Hold your phone upright for the full height. Take a second, tighter shot at 2x or more to pick out the wooden frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the crane to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the brick keeps its colour. Take a few frames in a row, because moving boats and passers-by change the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or evening usually gives softer light and fewer people on the quay. After dusk, try night mode with your phone braced against a railing or wall.

text.access_note: The crane stands on the Motława shore, but it houses a museum, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Main Town Hall
label: Main Town Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Długi Targ' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Długi Targ' (relation/5537950): middle (225 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/60064065: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museum of Gdansk' (61 m across).
notes: Tall Gothic-Renaissance tower with a view over the old town.

text.description:
Gdansk's Main Town Hall closes the far end of the Long Market, and its slim tower is the second-highest in the Main City after St Mary's Church. The building is Gothic-Renaissance in style. The oldest fragments date from 1327 to 1336, and the tower went up between 1486 and 1488. After a fire in 1556 the building was rebuilt with Renaissance touches by Dutch architects, and in 1561 a gilded weathervane figure of King Sigismund II Augustus was set on top. The town hall was badly damaged in the Second World War, including the loss of the top of the tower, and was largely rebuilt by 1952. Today it houses the city's history museum.

It photographs well because of the setting. From the Neptune Fountain end of the Long Market you get the tower at the end of the square, the fountain close by and the colourful tenement facades down both sides. That gives you a foreground, a middle and a clear focal point in one frame. Go early if you can. Café parasols and outdoor seating can clutter the scene in summer, and the square is far emptier at sunrise. Two other angles are worth a look: ulica Długa, with the facade at the end of a row of townhouses, and ulica Chlebnicka, which frames the town hall between its buildings. You do not need to climb the tower for any of these ground-level shots.
text.geographic_location: In the Main City (Główne Miasto) part of Gdansk's old town, where ulica Długa meets the Long Market (Długi Targ). It stands on the Royal Route, a short walk from the Neptune Fountain.
text.directions_text: Head for the Main City, the old town centre of Gdansk, and finish the journey on foot, since ulica Długa is pedestrianised all year. Public transport does not reach the building itself; the closest tram stop is Podwale Przedmiejskie. Walk to the Neptune Fountain end of the Long Market and the town hall is in front of you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic view down the square. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the fountain and the facades large in the foreground. A 2x or 3x telephoto lens, if your phone has one, isolates the tower and weathervane.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Długi Targ (from the Neptune Fountain end of the square, facing the town hall). The town hall tower closing the far end of the Long Market, with the Neptune Fountain and the colourful tenement facades in the foreground. Alternatives are ulica Długa, for the facade at the end of the townhouse row, and ulica Chlebnicka, where the buildings frame the town hall. For Chlebnicka you may need to walk the street to find the framing.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the tower on a vertical line so it stands straight. Keep the fountain low in the frame as a foreground. Hold the phone level, because tilting it up makes the buildings lean inwards. If people or parasols clutter the frame, wait a moment or move a few steps sideways.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the facades are not washed out. Take a few frames in a row, as people keep walking through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise, before the visitors and outdoor seating arrive. After rain, ulica Długa gives reflections on the wet paving.

text.access_note: The square and streets around the town hall are open public space, but the tower climb is paid and the museum may have its own ticketing, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: A 2x or 3x telephoto lens, where a phone has one, helps isolate the tower from the surrounding buildings.
Tilting the phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean inwards.
Lowering the exposure slightly helps keep sky colour and detail on a bright facade.

name: Great Armoury
label: Great Armoury
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1549228: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Dutch Mannerist arsenal facing Targ Węglowy.

text.description:
The Great Armoury is a former arsenal beside the Targ Węglowy (Coal Market) in Gdańsk, and it is one of the most striking façades on the square. It was built between 1600 and 1605 to a design by Anthonis van Obbergen, and it is described as the finest example of Mannerist architecture in the city. The designers took inspiration from the Vleeshal in Haarlem. It served as an arsenal until 1793. After severe damage in 1945 it was rebuilt between 1947 and 1951, and today it houses the Academy of Fine Arts. The old ground-floor passage has been used for art exhibitions since 2012.

It photographs well because of the roofline. Four gables stand side by side, and the gaps between them make the building look like four separate houses. Higher up the façade there are carved reliefs, including Athena, soldiers of Gdańsk and exploding cannonballs. These give you a wide shot of the whole front and close-up details to pick out.

The phone icon on the map is about 55 m south of the subject. That gives you room to fit the full façade in one frame. Take a wide shot first, then zoom in on the gables and carvings. Keep your phone upright so you do not cut off the tops of the gables.
text.geographic_location: The Great Armoury is beside the Targ Węglowy (Coal Market) in Gdańsk.
text.directions_text: Head for the Targ Węglowy in Gdańsk by whatever route suits you. Walk north from there and the façade will be in front of you. The phone icon on the map is about 55 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole façade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit all four gables in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved reliefs high on the front.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 55 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From here the whole front, with its four gables, fits in one view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the gables up with the top third of the frame. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight. If the whole building will not fit at 1x, use 0.5x, but keep the façade in the middle of the frame to limit stretching at the edges. For a second shot, zoom in on the gables and the carved figures.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few shots in case people walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people in the frame. Soft light in the morning or late afternoon, or on a bright overcast day, helps the carvings show without harsh shadows.

text.access_note: The façade can be photographed from the square outside; for exhibitions or the interior, check the official site before you go.

name: Golden Gate
label: Golden Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Targ Węglowy' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Targ Węglowy' (way/1120241552): middle (37 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/144731963: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Golden gate' (23 m across).
notes: Ornate gate with allegorical statues at the start of the Royal Way.

text.description: The Golden Gate is a handsome Renaissance city gate at the end of Ulica Długa, the start of the Royal Route through Gdańsk's Old Town. It was built in 1612-14 to replace a 13th-century Gothic gate, and it stands with the Highland Gate and the Prison Tower as part of the old city fortifications. The architect was Abraham van den Blocke, and the style is Dutch Mannerism. It photographs well because the front is rich in detail: the top of each side carries four statues, figures of qualities such as Peace, Freedom, Justice and Prudence, and a Latin motto runs across the gate. The statues were designed in 1648 and rebuilt in 1878 after weathering damaged the originals. Next to the gate is the late-Gothic Brotherhood of St. George building, which gives a good second layer to a wide shot. The gate was damaged by shelling in World War II but was not destroyed, and it was repaired in 1957. For the classic picture, stand on Targ Węglowy, the open square in front of the western face, and shoot the gate head-on. Keep the phone level so the arch and the statues stay straight. If you have time, take a second shot from Ulica Długa, where the gate closes the end of the long street. Plan to come in the evening: the gate looks especially good at sunset and once it is lit up at night.
text.geographic_location: The gate is in Gdańsk's Old Town, at the western end of Ulica Długa on the Royal Route. It sits beside the Brotherhood of St. George building, close to the Coal Market square (Targ Węglowy).
text.directions_text: There are no tram or train stops listed for this spot, so start from the Old Town or the Coal Market square and finish on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the head-on view of the whole gate. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is busy or you want the Brotherhood of St. George building in the frame too. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statues along the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Targ Węglowy (the open square in front of the gate's western face). The gate's front facade seen head-on from the Coal Market side, with the gilded statues and the neighbouring Brotherhood of St. George building. This western side is treated as the gate's main face, and it is where you enter the Royal Route from the old fortifications.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the centre of the arch with the middle grid line, keeping the phone upright so the verticals stay straight. Leave a little sky above the statues. Include the neighbouring Brotherhood of St. George building on one side. For a second view, walk to Ulica Długa and shoot the gate closing the end of the long, straight street, with the red brick of the Amber Museum rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out the stonework and gilding. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the shot sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening: around sunset, or later once the gate is lit up at night.

text.access_note: The gate is a public arch you can walk through, but the museum inside may be ticketed or have set hours, so check the official site before you go.

name: Green Gate
label: Green Gate
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/60064091: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Green Gate' (51 m across).
notes: Renaissance gate closing the Long Market on the Motława river side.

text.description:
The Green Gate is a handsome brick-and-stone gatehouse where Long Market meets the River Motława. It was built between 1568 and 1571 and shows clear Flemish influence. It was reportedly inspired by Antwerp City Hall, and it is one of the gates of the Royal Route. It was meant as a residence for Poland's monarchs, though the king never actually stayed here. Today it houses the National Museum in Gdańsk, and the office of former President Lech Wałęsa is in one of its rooms.

It photographs well because it has a strong symmetrical front, several arches and a busy skyline of rooftops and small towers, with the water close by. The phone icon on the map is about 130 m east of the subject. This is a good place for a straightforward 'we were here' photo. It also gives you a few minutes to try a closer shot of the arches and stonework. Passers-by are likely to cross your view at busy times, so take a few frames and pick the cleanest. Stay out of the roadway and the way of other visitors while you line up the shot.
text.geographic_location: In Gdańsk, between Long Market (Długi Targ) and the River Motława.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot; head for Long Market and walk to the river end. The gate stands at the river end of Long Market. The phone icon on the map is about 130 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole gate and some of its surroundings. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the arches, windows and rooftop decoration. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if people or railings are in the way and you need to step back, and keep the building well away from the edges of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 130 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. From there the gate's whole front is in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the gate's vertical edges parallel to the lines so the towers do not lean. Hold the phone level, then crop a little later if needed. For a second picture, zoom in on the central arch and the roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the brickwork keeps its colour. Hold the phone steady with both hands, with your elbows against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or earlier in the day should suit the phone icon on the map best, since the light then comes from behind you. On an overcast day the light is even and the colours of the brick still look good.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from public space, but the building is a museum, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Long Street (Długa)
label: Long Street
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Długa Street, Gdańsk'.
notes: The historic Royal Way lined with ornate facades.

text.description:
Long Street (Długa), also called the Long Lane, is a famous street in Gdańsk's historic centre, part of the Royal Route and one of the city's best-known tourist sights. It leads from the Golden Gate (Złota Brama) to the Długi Targ (Long Market) and the Green Gate (Brama Zielona). Along the way you pass named houses such as Ferber House, Schumann House, Uphagen House and Lion Castle.

For a phone photographer the appeal is the view along the street. The fronts of the tall, narrow houses line up on both sides and lead the eye towards the end of the street, so a simple, straight-on shot already has depth and a clear subject. Walkers passing through add scale and life, and shopfront details and carved facades make good close-ups once you have your wide view.

Keep your phone upright to capture the full height of the facades, and use the gridlines to keep the buildings straight. Let a few people walk into the frame rather than waiting for an empty street, as this is a busy place. If you want to photograph a particular house, walk up to it and take a second shot with the default lens (1x), or the telephoto if your phone has one, for the doorway and decoration.
text.geographic_location: Long Street lies in the historic city centre of Gdańsk, leading from the Golden Gate to the Długi Targ (Long Market) and the Green Gate.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop right at this spot, so start from the historic city centre of Gdańsk, around the Golden Gate or the Długi Targ and Green Gate, the places the street leads between. The phone icon on the map is about 85 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view down the street. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the full height of the facades, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a doorway or a house front.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 85 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the house fronts with the vertical lines so they stand straight. Place the street in the middle of the frame so the facades on both sides lead towards the end. Hold the phone level and a little above chest height to avoid tilted buildings. For a close-up, use the telephoto on one facade or doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the buildings to focus and lower the exposure slider slightly, so the sky does not wash out and the colours of the facades stay rich. Try a Live Photo to catch people walking through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning is usually quieter, and softer light is kinder to the facades. Later in the day the street is busier, which gives more life but more people in your frame.

text.access_note: The street is a public thoroughfare in the historic centre; for any of the houses along it that you want to enter, check the official site before you go.

name: Basilica of St. Nicholas
label: St. Nicholas Basilica
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'ulica Lawendowa' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of ulica Lawendowa nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/240128505: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bazylika Świętego Mikołaja' (75 m across).
notes: Dominican church, one of the few to survive WWII unscathed.

text.description:
St Nicholas's is a Brick Gothic church in Gdańsk's Old Town, built between the 14th and 15th centuries and still run by the Dominican Order. Its plain red brick and tall roofline look more like a fortress than a church, and that is what makes it work in a photo. It is also the only historic church in central Gdańsk that came through the Second World War undamaged, which is why the interior still holds Gothic to Rococo furnishings. The church is about 63 metres long.

The viewpoint on the map is on ulica Lawendowa. From here you see the basilica's side elevation framed by the houses along the street, which is a less usual angle. The church was closed in 2018 when cracks appeared in the vaulting, and repair work on the foundations and vaults was finished by 2022. Scaffolding may still be on this side, so it may be in your picture. Check what is there when you arrive and, if it is in the way, try the second viewpoint at Świętojańska and Szeroka. From that open square you get a clear view of the brick Gothic exterior.

Keep your phone level so the walls and the house fronts stay straight, and use the gridlines to help. Step back to the far side of the street to fit more in. If you go inside, visitor guides say photography is fine without flash and outside service times.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Town of Gdańsk.
text.directions_text: Navigate on foot to the basilica in the Old Town of Gdańsk. Head for the basilica for the last stretch. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the basilica and the houses on either side. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for brick, windows and roof details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on ulica Lawendowa. The basilica's side elevation with scaffolding, framed by the houses along Lawendowa street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the houses on both sides of the street as a frame and keep the church in the middle of the picture. Turn on gridlines and keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight. If scaffolding blocks the view, take a tighter shot with the telephoto of the brickwork and tower, or walk to Świętojańska and Szeroka for a clear view of the exterior from the open square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright so the red brick keeps its colour. Inside, switch the flash off.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light tends to flatter red brick. Go early if you want the street to yourself.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the street, but the basilica is a working place of worship (dress modestly, and expect limits during services), so check the official site before you go for opening times and for the crypt.

name: Prison Tower and Torture Chamber
label: Prison Tower
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/374156466: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Katownia' (22 m across).
notes: Medieval tower and torture chamber next to the Golden Gate.

text.description: The Torture Chamber (Katownia in Polish) is a red-roofed building, one of the old city gates, with a tall, copper-topped tower at one end. Its two-sided roof and the carved busts that stick out of the walls give you plenty of texture and detail to work with. It was a prison for much of its history, which is where the name comes from. The building went up beside the city walls in the 14th century. It became obsolete when new fortifications, including the Highland Gate, were built in the late 16th century. It was then rebuilt and enlarged by the architect Anthonis van Obbergen between 1593 and 1604, and it stayed the municipal prison until 1861. One of the busts lost its head in 1945, which is an odd detail to look for if you zoom in. An amber museum used the building from 2006 until 2021, and it currently has no fixed use. For a phone photo, the tower and the long roofline are the main subjects. Stand back far enough to fit both in, then take a second shot zoomed in on the busts and walls. Keep the vertical lines straight with the gridlines. If people walk into the frame, wait a moment for a clear shot.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Gdańsk, on the line of the old city defences, in the area of the Highland Gate.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are close by, so head for the Highland Gate area in central Gdańsk; it is an easy walk within central Gdańsk. The Torture Chamber is in the same area as the Highland Gate. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because you are standing close to a long building with a tall tower. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view, and 2x-5x for the busts and the copper top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone to landscape to take in the roofline and tower together, then switch to portrait orientation for a tall shot of the tower alone. Turn on the gridlines and line the walls and tower up with the vertical lines. Because you are so close, tilting the phone up makes the tower lean inwards. Hold it level, step back if you can, and leave some space above to crop later. Then zoom in to 2x-5x for details such as the carved busts.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the red roof to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the roof keeps its colour. Turn on the gridlines to keep the verticals straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even light on a bright overcast day suits the red roof, and morning or late afternoon gives more warmth. Check where the sun is on the day, because shooting straight into it will turn the tower into a silhouette.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the surrounding streets, but the building currently has no fixed public use, so check the official site before you go if you hope to go inside.

name: Granary Island
label: Granary Island
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/707953191: large area 'Wyspa Spichrzów' (1021 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Island of old granaries opposite the Green Gate, with views of the old town.

text.description: Granary Island is the strip of land just east of Gdansk's Main City, with the Motława river on one side and the New Motława on the other. It photographs well because you get water, old brick-and-timber warehouse shapes and the Main City skyline across the river in a single view. Granaries have stood on this bank since the 14th century, and at one time there were as many as 300. The island itself only appeared in 1576, when the New Motława was dug out. Much of the northern part was lost in March 1945 during the siege, so today old and new buildings sit side by side. Some of the granaries that remain are the Blue Lamb (Błękitny Baranek), now part of the Archaeological Museum, and Deo Gloria, built into a modern row of buildings. The Milk can Gate (Brama Stągiewna), from 1517-1519, is another good subject. For photos, look for the reflections along the river and the lines of rooftops and gables. Include a bit of the water in the foreground to give the picture depth. Bridges such as the Green Bridge and the Cow Bridge make natural frames. Take a few wide shots for the scene, then closer ones of brickwork, gates and gables.
text.geographic_location: Granary Island is in Śródmieście, the central district of Gdansk, just east of the Main City. It lies between the Motława and the New Motława.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the Main City around Long Market and the Green Gate; the Green Bridge (Zielony Most) crosses the Motława from there to the island. The phone icon on the map is about 90 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the river, the bridge and the granaries together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the water and want the whole row of buildings. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for gables, brick details and the Milk can Gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 90 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon straight, because the water and rooflines show any tilt. Put the river across the lower third and the granaries above it. A bridge or a gate at the edge of the picture makes a good frame. Take one wide shot, then a closer one of a single building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the building front to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the brickwork stays rich. If the water is moving, try a Live Photo and pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the brick and calmer streets. After dusk, night mode can capture lit buildings reflected in the river; rest your elbows on a rail to keep the phone steady.

text.access_note: The island and its riverside are open public space, but individual buildings such as the museum may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the brick buildings.
Streets are usually quieter in the morning.
The river can give reflections of the buildings, especially on calm days and after dusk.
The island and riverside are generally open public space that you can walk around.
The Main City skyline is visible from the river bank near the island.

name: SS Sołdek
label: SS Sołdek
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ołowianka' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Ołowianka nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/125199669: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'SS Sołdek' (88 m across).
notes: Museum ship moored on the Motława.

text.description:
SS Sołdek is a retired coal and ore steamship, now a museum ship moored on the Motława river beside the old granaries. She was the first ship built in Gdańsk after the Second World War and the first seagoing ship completed in Poland. She was also the first of 29 ships of the Project B30 type, built at the Gdańsk Shipyard between 1949 and 1954. Her name honours Stanisław Sołdek, one of the shipyard's shock workers. She has also appeared on screen, playing a Japanese steamer in the film Persona Non Grata.

She photographs well because the red-and-black hull stands out against the granary walls and the water, with the Old Town skyline behind. From the quayside you can fit the whole ship into one frame without paying for entry. Stand on the quay, keep the hull level with the gridlines, and leave a little water in the foreground so the ship looks moored rather than cropped. If you want to show the granaries and skyline too, step back along the quay before you switch lenses. For a second view, the east bank at Długie Pobrzeże shows the ship across the river, with the Crane and the Main Town waterfront houses in the same shot. Boarding the ship is a separate matter. Photography is banned inside the 'Sołdek and its Times' exhibition, so enjoy the outside views and keep the phone in your pocket indoors.
text.geographic_location: On the Ołowianka waterfront beside the Motława river, in front of the granaries, across the water from Gdańsk's Main Town. The ship is moored directly alongside the quay.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is close to the ship, so head to the Ołowianka waterfront beside the granaries (on foot from the Main Town side). The ship is moored in front of them. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the full hull against the granaries and river. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the quay is crowded or you cannot step back far enough. Use telephoto (2x or more) to pick out details such as the funnel, rigging or bow.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ołowianka (quayside directly in front of the ship, on the Motława waterfront beside the granaries). The full hull of the red-and-black freighter moored against the granary facades and the river, with the Old Town skyline behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the gridlines on and place the waterline along the lower line so the hull sits steady in the frame. Include a strip of water in front. If you want a different angle, the east bank at Długie Pobrzeże shows the ship across the river with the Crane and the Main Town houses.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red hull to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky and water keep their colour and the dark paintwork does not wash out. Keep your phone away from the edge of the quay.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides recommend morning, when the sun lights the waterfront and the ship.

text.access_note: The quayside is free to stand on, but going aboard the ship is ticketed, so check the official site before you go; photography is not allowed in the 'Sołdek and its Times' exhibition.
